rv.q: This is a Rolls Royce of a revival, precision-tooled and carrying the weight of the show’s history lightly.

As Eliza Doolittle, the 25-year-old gives one of the most enthralling stage performances of the year, transforming from a gobby Cockney flower seller to a member of the genteel English middle classes at the hands of Professor Henry Higgins (Harry Hadden-Paton).
This Bartlett Sher production is unashamedly sensuous.

Almost everything else, unfortunately, is problematic.
In particular, this revival owes the most to its gently assured lead performances...
Nevertheless, it is all part of the theatricality that drives this production of what must be the most English of American musicals.
This is a thoughtful grappling with a rich and complex musical, balancing old-fashioned charm with fresh ideas, and, at its best, blossoming into a truly loverly night out.
It’s an assured revival, and it’s a largely faithful one...

She shimmers like sunshine as she sings to the dawn in "I Could Have Danced All Night", and grounds the whole three-hour show with a faultless depiction of someone simply wanting to get ahead in the world.
But whilst many scenes delight, the end resuly doesn’t’ deliver a strong or engaged narrative.
The show is packed with beautiful, familiar tunes, but over all, lacks energy and anything new to say.
Amara Okereke blossoms in the role of Eliza, from humble flower girl to debutante, Okereke’s performance is flawless and utterly captivating.
A great musical expertly done with laugh out moments.
Sher gives Doolittle the respect she deserves after she’s belittled by two men – and the musical is still the same rollickingly effective comment on classism as it ever was.
Indeed, the whole production and pacing is a little too elegant, gliding elegantly along like a swan you might admire on a nearby river, but never really making a splash.
I pitied the cast whose gallant efforts to make this antediluvian theatre production engaging deserved the most credit.
Its charming cast and traditional production are certainly worthy and will guarantee an evening full of wonderful music.

cn.t: Bartlett Sher's Broadway revival earns mostly warm notices, with Amara Okereke's Eliza Doolittle drawing consistent praise, though some critics find the production safe and lacking energy.
